International relations
As of 2023, the City of Sacramento has 14 <color=#3366CC>sister cities</color>. They are:
South Asia
South Asia is the southern sub-region of <color=#3366CC>Asia</color> that is defined in both geographical and <color=#3366CC>ethnic</color>-<color=#3366CC>cultural</color> terms. South Asia,
with a population of 2.04 billion, contains a quarter (25%) of the world's population. As commonly conceptualised, the

modern <color=#3366CC>states</color> of South Asia include <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color>, <color=#3366CC>India</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Maldives</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color>, with
<color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> also often included, which may also be classified as part of <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>. South Asia borders <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> to
the northeast, Central Asia to the northwest, <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> to the west and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> to the east. Southeast Asia and
Maritime South Asia are the only subregions of Asia that lie partly within the <color=#3366CC>Southern Hemisphere</color>. The <color=#3366CC>British Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ocean Territory</color> and two out of <color=#3366CC>26 atolls</color> of the Maldives in South Asia lie entirely within the Southern Hemisphere.
Topographically, it is dominated by the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> and is bounded by the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color> in the south, and the
<color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Karakoram</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Pamir Mountains</color> in the north.
<color=#3366CC>Settled life</color> emerged on the Indian subcontinent in the western margins of the <color=#3366CC>Indus River</color> Basin 9,000 years ago,
evolving gradually into the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilisation</color> of the third millennium BCE. By, an <color=#3366CC>archaic form</color> of <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color>, an
<color=#3366CC>Indo-European language</color>, had <color=#3366CC>diffused</color> into India from the northwest, with the <color=#3366CC>Dravidian languages</color> being supplanted in
the northern and western regions. By, <color=#3366CC>stratification</color> and exclusion by <color=#3366CC>caste</color> had emerged within <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> had arisen, proclaiming <color=#3366CC>social orders</color> unlinked to heredity.

In the early medieval era, <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> became established on South Asia's
southern and western coasts. <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color> armies from Central Asia intermittently overran the plains of northern India,
eventually founding the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color> in the 13th century, and drawing the region into the cosmopolitan <color=#3366CC>networks of</color>
<color=#3366CC>medieval Islam</color>. The Islamic <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color>, in 1526, ushered in two centuries of relative peace, leaving a legacy of
luminous architecture. Gradually expanding rule of the British East India Company followed, turning most of South Asia
into a colonial economy, but also consolidating its <color=#3366CC>sovereignty</color>. <color=#3366CC>British Crown rule</color> began in 1858. The rights promised
to Indians were granted slowly, but <color=#3366CC>technological changes</color> were introduced, and modern ideas of education and the
public life took root. In 1947, the <color=#3366CC>British Indian Empire</color> was <color=#3366CC>partitioned</color> into two independent dominions, a
Hindu-majority Dominion of India and a Muslim-majority Dominion of Pakistan, amid large-scale loss of life and an
unprecedented migration. The 1971 <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh Liberation War</color>, a Cold War episode resulting in East Pakistan's
secession, was the most recent instance of a new nation being formed in the region.
South Asia has a total area of 5.2 million km2 (2 million sq.mi), which is 10% of the Asian continent. The population of
South Asia is estimated to be 2.04 billion or about one-fourth of the world's population, making it both the most
populous and the <color=#3366CC>most densely populated</color> geographical region in the world.
In 2022, South Asia had the world's largest populations of <color=#3366CC>Hindus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>, Sikhs, Jains, and Zoroastrians. South Asia
alone accounts for 90.47% of Hindus, 95.5% of Sikhs, and 31% of Muslims worldwide, as well as 35 million <color=#3366CC>Christians</color>
and 25 million Buddhists.
The <color=#3366CC>South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation</color> (SAARC) is an economic cooperation organisation in the region
which was established in 1985 and includes all of the South Asian nations.
Definition
Ambiguity
The geographical extent is not clear cut as systemic and foreign policy orientations of its constituents are quite
asymmetrical. Beyond the core territories of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Empire</color> (territories of the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> which were under the
system of British Raj), there is a high degree of variation as to which other countries are included in South Asia. There
is no clear boundary – geographical, geopolitical, socio-cultural, economical, or historical – between South Asia and
other parts of Asia, especially Southeast Asia and West Asia. Most of this region is peninsular, resting on the Indian
Plate and being isolated from the rest of Asia by mountain barriers; it resembles a diamond which is delineated by the
Himalayas on the north, the <color=#3366CC>Hindu Kush</color> in the west, and the Arakanese in the east, and which extends southward into
the Indian Ocean with the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Sea</color> to the southwest and the <color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color> to the southeast.
The common definition of South Asia is largely inherited from the administrative boundaries of the Indian Empire, with
several exceptions. The current territories of <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>, <color=#3366CC>India</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> which were the core territories of the
<color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> from 1857 to 1947 also form the core territories of South Asia. The mountain countries of <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color>, two independent countries that were not under the British Raj but were protectorates of the Empire, and the
island countries of Sri Lanka and the Maldives are generally included. By various definitions based on substantially
different reasons, the <color=#3366CC>British Indian Ocean Territory</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Tibet Autonomous Region</color> may be included as well.
<color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color> (Burma), a former British colony and now largely considered a part of Southeast Asia, is also sometimes
included. <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> is also included by some sources.
Organisational definitions
The <color=#3366CC>South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation</color> (SAARC), a contiguous block of countries, started in 1985 with
seven countries – Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka – and admitted Afghanistan
as an eighth member in 2007. China and Myanmar have also applied for the status of full members of SAARC. The
South Asia Free Trade Agreement admitted Afghanistan in 2011.
The <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> and <color=#3366CC>United Nations Children's Fund</color> (UNICEF) recognises the eight SAARC countries as South Asia,
while the Hirschman–Herfindahl index of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific
for the region excludes Afghanistan from South Asia. Population Information Network (POPIN) excludes Maldives
which is included as a member Pacific POPIN subregional network. The United Nations Statistics Division's scheme of
subregions, for statistical purpose, includes <color=#3366CC>Iran</color> along with all eight members of the SAARC as part of Southern Asia.
Indian subcontinent
The terms "<color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>" and "South Asia" are sometimes used interchangeably. The Indian subcontinent is
largely a geological term referring to the land mass that drifted northeastwards from ancient <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>, colliding with
the Eurasian plate nearly 55 million years ago, towards the end of Palaeocene. This geological region largely includes
Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. Historians Catherine Asher and Cynthia Talbot
state that the term "Indian subcontinent" describes a natural physical landmass in South Asia that has been relatively
isolated from the rest of Eurasia.
The use of the term Indian subcontinent began in the British Empire, and has been a term particularly common in its
successors. South Asia as the preferred term is particularly common when scholars or officials seek to differentiate this
region from East Asia. According to historians Sugata Bose and Ayesha Jalal, the Indian subcontinent has come to be
known as South Asia "in more recent and neutral parlance." This "neutral" notion refers to the concerns of Pakistan and
Bangladesh, particularly given the recurring conflicts between India and Pakistan, wherein the dominant placement of
"India" as a prefix before the subcontinent might offend some political sentiments. In Pakistan, even the term "South
Asia" was considered too India-centric and was "banned" within the International Relations department of Karachi
University until 1989 after the death of <color=#3366CC>Zia ul Haq</color>. This region has also been labelled as "India" (in its classical and
<color=#3366CC>pre-modern</color> sense) and "<color=#3366CC>Greater India</color>".
Asian context
According to Robert M. Cutler – a scholar of political science at Carleton University, the terms South Asia, Southwest
Asia, and Central Asia are distinct, but the confusion and disagreements have arisen due to the geopolitical movement
to enlarge these regions into Greater South Asia, Greater Southwest Asia, and Greater Central Asia. The frontier of
Greater South Asia, states Cutler, between 2001 and 2006 has been geopolitically extended to eastern Iran and
western Afghanistan in the west, and in the north to northeastern Iran, northern Afghanistan, and southern <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color>.
Identification with a South Asian identity was found to be significantly low among respondents in an older two-year
survey across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka.
History
Pre-history
The history of core South Asia begins with evidence of human activity of <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color>, as long as 75,000 years ago,
or with earlier hominids including <color=#3366CC>Homo erectus</color> from about 500,000 years ago. The earliest prehistoric culture have
roots in the <color=#3366CC>Mesolithic</color> sites as evidenced by the rock paintings of <color=#3366CC>Bhimbetka rock shelters</color> dating to a period of 30,000
BCE or older, as well as Neolithic times.
Ancient era
The <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilisation</color>, which spread and flourished in the northwestern part of South Asia from c. 3300 to 1300
BCE in present-day <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>North India</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>, was the first major civilisation in South Asia. A
sophisticated and technologically advanced urban culture developed in the <color=#3366CC>Mature Harappan</color> period, from 2600 to 1900
BCE. According to anthropologist Possehl, the Indus Valley Civilisation provides a logical, if somewhat arbitrary,
starting point for South Asian religions, but these links from the Indus religion to later-day South Asian traditions are
subject to scholarly dispute.
The Vedic period, named after the Vedic religion of the <color=#3366CC>Indo-Aryans</color>, lasted from c. 1900 to 500 BCE. The Indo-Aryans
were <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color>-speaking pastoralists who migrated into north-western India after the collapse of the Indus Valley
Civilisation. Linguistic and archaeological data show a cultural change after 1500 BCE, with the linguistic and religious
data showing links with Indo-European languages and religion. By about 1200 BCE, the Vedic culture and agrarian
lifestyle were established in the northwest and northern Gangetic plain of South Asia. Rudimentary state-forms
appeared, of which the <color=#3366CC>Kuru</color>-Pañcāla union was the most influential. The first recorded <color=#3366CC>state-level society</color> in South Asia
existed around 1000 BCE. The <color=#3366CC>Brahmanas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Aranyakas</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Upanishads</color> into which they merged, began to ask
the meaning of a ritual, adding increasing levels of philosophical and metaphysical speculation, or "<color=#3366CC>Hindu synthesis</color>".
Increasing urbanisation of South Asia between 800 and 400 BCE, and possibly the spread of urban diseases,
contributed to the rise of ascetic movements and of new ideas which challenged the orthodox <color=#3366CC>Brahmanism</color>. These

ideas led to <color=#3366CC>Śramana</color> movements, of which <color=#3366CC>Mahavira</color> (c. 549–477 BCE), proponent of <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Buddha</color> (c. 563 – c.
483), founder of <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, were the most prominent icons.
The Greek army led by <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> stayed in the <color=#3366CC>Hindu Kush</color> region of South Asia for several years and then
later moved into the Indus valley region. Later, the <color=#3366CC>Maurya Empire</color> extended over much of South Asia in the 3rd century
BCE. Buddhism spread beyond South Asia, through northwest into Central Asia. The <color=#3366CC>Bamiyan Buddhas</color> of Afghanistan
and the <color=#3366CC>Edicts of Ashoka</color> suggest that the Buddhist monks spread Buddhism (Dharma) in eastern provinces of the
<color=#3366CC>Seleucid Empire</color>, and possibly even farther into West Asia. The Theravada school spread south from India in the 3rd
century BCE, to Sri Lanka, later to Southeast Asia. Buddhism, by the last centuries of the 1st millennium BCE, was
prominent in the Himalayan region, Gandhara, Hindu Kush region, and Bactria.
From about 500 BCE through about 300 CE, the Vedic-Brahmanic synthesis or "Hindu synthesis" continued. Classical
Hindu and Sramanic (particularly Buddhist) ideas spread within South Asia, as well as outside South Asia. The <color=#3366CC>Gupta</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> ruled over a large part of the region between the 4th and 7th centuries, a period that saw the construction of
major temples, monasteries and universities such as the <color=#3366CC>Nalanda</color>. During this era, and through the 10th century,
numerous cave monasteries and temples such as the <color=#3366CC>Ajanta Caves</color>, Badami cave temples, and <color=#3366CC>Ellora Caves</color> were built
in South Asia.
Medieval era
Islam came as a political power in the fringe of South Asia in 8th century CE when the Arab general Muhammad bin
Qasim conquered <color=#3366CC>Sindh</color> and <color=#3366CC>Multan</color> in southern Punjab, in modern-day Pakistan. By 962 CE, Hindu and Buddhist
kingdoms in South Asia were under a wave of raids from Muslim armies from Central Asia. Among them was <color=#3366CC>Mahmud</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Ghazni</color>, who raided and plundered kingdoms in north India from east of the Indus river to west of Yamuna river
seventeen times between 997 and 1030. Mahmud of Ghazni raided the treasuries but retracted each time, only
extending Islamic rule into western Punjab.
The wave of raids on north Indian and western Indian kingdoms by Muslim warlords continued after Mahmud of
Ghazni, plundering and looting these kingdoms. The raids did not establish or extend permanent boundaries of their
Islamic kingdoms. The Ghurid Sultan <color=#3366CC>Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad</color> began a systematic war of expansion into North India in
1173. He sought to carve out a principality for himself by expanding the Islamic world, and thus laid the foundation for
the Muslim kingdom that became the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>. Some historians chronicle the Delhi Sultanate from 1192 due to
the presence and geographical claims of Mu'izz al-Din in South Asia by that time.
The Delhi Sultanate covered varying parts of South Asia and was ruled by a series of dynasties: Mamluk, Khalji,
Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties. <color=#3366CC>Muhammad bin Tughlaq</color> came to power in 1325, launched a war of expansion
and the Delhi Sultanate reached it largest geographical reach over the South Asian region during his 26-year rule. A
Sunni Sultan, Muhammad bin Tughlaq persecuted non-Muslims such as Hindus, as well as non-Sunni Muslims such as
Shia and Mahdi sects.
Revolts against the Delhi Sultanate sprang up in many parts of South Asia during the 14th century. In the northeast, the
<color=#3366CC>Bengal Sultanate</color> became independent in 1346 CE. It remained in power through the early 16th century. The state
religion of the sultanate was Islam. In <color=#3366CC>South India</color>, the Hindu <color=#3366CC>Vijayanagara Empire</color> came to power in 1336 and
persisted until the middle of the 16th century. It was ultimately defeated and destroyed by an alliance of the Muslim
<color=#3366CC>Deccan sultanates</color> at the Battle of Talikota.
About 1526, the Punjab governor Daulat Khan Lodi reached out to the Mughal <color=#3366CC>Babur</color> and invited him to attack the Delhi
Sultanate. Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Panipat</color> in 1526. The death of Ibrahim Lodi ended the
Delhi Sultanate, and the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> replaced it.
Modern era
The <color=#3366CC>modern history period</color> of South Asia, that is the 16th century onwards, witnessed the establishment of the Mughal
Empire, with Sunni Islam theology. The first ruler was Babur had Turco-Mongol roots and his realm included the
northwestern and <color=#3366CC>Indo-Gangetic Plain</color> regions of South Asia. Several regions of South Asia were largely under Hindu
kings such as those of the <color=#3366CC>Vijayanagara Empire</color> and the Kingdom of Mewar. Parts of modern <color=#3366CC>Telangana</color> and <color=#3366CC>Andhra</color>
<color=#3366CC>Pradesh</color> were under local Muslim rulers, the Deccan Sutanates.
The Mughal Empire continued its wars of expansion after Babur's death. With the fall of the Rajput kingdoms and
Vijayanagara, its boundaries encompassed almost the entirety of the Indian subcontinent. The Mughal Empire was
marked by a period of artistic exchanges and a Central Asian and South Asian architecture synthesis, with remarkable
buildings such as the <color=#3366CC>Taj Mahal</color>.
However, this time also marked an extended period of <color=#3366CC>religious persecution</color>. Two of the religious leaders of <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Guru Arjan</color>, and Guru Tegh Bahadur were arrested under orders of the Mughal emperors after their revolts and were
executed when they refused to convert to Islam. Religious taxes on non-Muslims called jizya were imposed. Buddhist,
Hindu, and Sikh temples were desecrated. However, not all Muslim rulers persecuted non-Muslims. <color=#3366CC>Akbar</color>, a Mughal
ruler for example, sought religious tolerance and abolished jizya.
The death of <color=#3366CC>Aurangzeb</color> and the collapse of the Mughal Empire, which marks the beginning of modern India, in the

early 18th century, provided opportunities for the <color=#3366CC>Marathas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sikhs</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mysoreans</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Nawabs of Bengal</color> to exercise
control over large regions of the Indian subcontinent. By the mid-18th century, India was a major proto-industrializing
region.
Maritime trading between South Asia and European merchants began at the turn of the 16th century after the
Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India. British, French, and Portuguese colonial interests struck treaties with
these rulers and established their trading ports. In northwestern South Asia, a large region was consolidated into the
Sikh Empire by <color=#3366CC>Ranjit Singh</color>. After the defeat of the <color=#3366CC>Nawab of Bengal</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tipu Sultan</color> and his French allies, British
traders went on to dominate much of South Asia through <color=#3366CC>divide and rule</color> tactics by the early 19th century. The region
experienced significant de-industrialisation in its first few decades of British rule. Control over the subcontinent was
then <color=#3366CC>transferred</color> to the British government after the <color=#3366CC>Indian Rebellion of 1857</color>, with the British cracking down to some
extent afterwards.
An increase of famines and extreme poverty characterised the colonial period, though railways built with British
technology eventually provided crucial famine relief by increasing food distribution throughout India. Millions of South
Asians began to migrate throughout the world, impelled by the economic/labour needs and opportunities presented by
the British Empire. The introduction of Western political thought inspired a growing Indian intellectual movement, and
so by the 20th century, British rule began to be challenged by the <color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color>, which sought full
independence under the leadership of <color=#3366CC>Mahatma Gandhi</color>.
Britain, under pressure from Indian freedom fighters, increasingly gave self-rule to British India. By the 1940s, two rival
camps had emerged among independence activists: those who favored a separate nation for Indian Muslims, and
those who wanted a united India. As <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> raged, over 2 million Indians fought for Britain; by the end of the war,
Britain was greatly weakened, and thus decided to grant independence to the vast majority of South Asians in 1947,
though this coincided with the <color=#3366CC>Partition of India</color> into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, which
resulted in significant displacement and violence and harder religious divides in the region.
Contemporary era
In 1947, the newly independent India and Pakistan had to decide how to deal with the hundreds of <color=#3366CC>princely states</color> that
controlled much of the subcontinent, as well as what to do with the remaining European (non-British) colonies. A
combination of referendums, military action, and negotiated accessions took place in rapid succession, leading to the
political integration of the vast majority of India and Pakistan within a few years. India and Pakistan <color=#3366CC>clashed several</color>
<color=#3366CC>times</color> in the decades after independence, with <color=#3366CC>disputes over Kashmir</color> playing a significant role. In 1971, the eastern half
of Pakistan seceded with help from India and became the People's Republic of Bangladesh after the traumatic
<color=#3366CC>Bangladesh Liberation War</color>. This, along with India and Pakistan gaining nuclear weapons soon afterwards, increased
tensions between the two countries. The <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> decades also contributed to the divide, as Pakistan aligned with the
West and India with the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>; other factors include the time period after the 1962 <color=#3366CC>Sino-Indian War</color>, which saw
India and China move apart while Pakistan and China built closer relations.
Pakistan has been beset with terrorism, economic issues, and military dominance of its government since
independence, with none of its Prime Ministers having completed a full 5-year term in office. India has grown
significantly, having slashed its rate of extreme poverty to below 20% and surpassed Pakistan's GDP per capita in the
2010s due to economic liberalisation from the 1980s onward. Bangladesh, having struggled greatly for decades due to
conflict with and economic exploitation by Pakistan, is now one of the fastest-growing countries in the region, beating
India in terms of <color=#3366CC>GDP per capita</color>. Afghanistan has gone through several invasions and Islamist regimes, with many of
its refugees having gone to Pakistan and other parts of South Asia and bringing back cultural influences such as
<color=#3366CC>cricket</color>. Religious nationalism has grown across the region, with persecution causing millions of Hindus and Christians
to flee Pakistan and Bangladesh, and <color=#3366CC>Hindu nationalism</color> having grown in India with the election of the <color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata</color>
<color=#3366CC>Party</color> in 2014.
A recent phenomenon has been that of India and China fighting on their border, as well as vying for dominance of
South Asia, with China partnering with Pakistan and using its superior economy to attract countries surrounding India,
while the United States and other countries have strengthened ties with India to counter China in the broader
Indo-Pacific. (See also: 2025 India–Pakistan standoff)
Geography
According to Saul Cohen, early colonial era strategists treated South Asia with East Asia, but in reality, the South Asia
region excluding Afghanistan is a distinct <color=#3366CC>geopolitical</color> region separated from other nearby geostrategic realms, one that
is geographically diverse. The region is home to a variety of geographical features, such as <color=#3366CC>glaciers</color>, <color=#3366CC>rainforests</color>,
<color=#3366CC>valleys</color>, <color=#3366CC>deserts</color>, and <color=#3366CC>grasslands</color> that are typical of much larger continents. It is surrounded by three water bodies – the
<color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color>, the Indian Ocean and the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Sea</color> – and has acutely varied climate zones. The tip of the Indian
Peninsula had the highest quality pearls.
Indian Plate
Most of this region is resting on the Indian Plate, the northerly portion of the <color=#3366CC>Indo-Australian Plate</color>, separated from the
rest of the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Plate</color>. The Indian Plate includes most of South Asia, forming a land mass which extends from the
<color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> into a portion of the basin under the Indian Ocean, including parts of <color=#3366CC>South China</color> and Eastern <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, as
well as <color=#3366CC>Kunlun</color> and <color=#3366CC>Karakoram</color> ranges, and extending up to but not including Ladakh, Kohistan, the <color=#3366CC>Hindu Kush</color> range,
and <color=#3366CC>Balochistan</color>. It may be noted that <color=#3366CC>geophysically</color> the <color=#3366CC>Yarlung Tsangpo River</color> in Tibet is situated at the outside the
border of the regional structure, while the <color=#3366CC>Pamir Mountains</color> in Tajikistan are situated inside that border.
The <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> formerly formed part of the <color=#3366CC>supercontinent</color> <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>, before rifting away during the
<color=#3366CC>Cretaceous</color> period and colliding with the Eurasian Plate about 50–55 million years ago and giving birth to the

<color=#3366CC>Himalayan range</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Plateau</color>. It is the <color=#3366CC>peninsular</color> region south of the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Kuen Lun</color> mountain
ranges and east of the <color=#3366CC>Indus River</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Iranian Plateau</color>, extending southward into the Indian Ocean between the
Arabian Sea (to the southwest) and the Bay of Bengal (to the southeast).
Climate
The climate of this vast region varies considerably from area to area from tropical monsoon in the south to temperate in
the north. The variety is influenced by not only the altitude but also by factors such as proximity to the seacoast and the
seasonal impact of the <color=#3366CC>monsoons</color>. Southern parts are mostly hot in summers and receive rain during monsoon periods.
The northern belt of <color=#3366CC>Indo-Gangetic plains</color> also is hot in summer, but cooler in winter. The mountainous north is colder
and receives snowfall at higher altitudes of Himalayan ranges.
As the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> block the north-Asian bitter cold winds, the temperatures are considerably moderate in the plains
down below. For the most part, the climate of the region is called the monsoon climate, which keeps the region humid
during summer and dry during winter, and favours the cultivation of <color=#3366CC>jute</color>, tea, rice, and various vegetables in this region.
South Asia is largely divided into four broad climate zones:
• The northern Indian edge and northern Pakistani uplands have a dry subtropical <color=#3366CC>continental climate</color>
• The far south of India and southwest Sri Lanka have an <color=#3366CC>equatorial climate</color>
• Most of the peninsula has a tropical climate with variations:
• Hot <color=#3366CC>subtropical</color> climate in northwest India
• Cool winter hot <color=#3366CC>tropical climate</color> in Bangladesh
• Tropical <color=#3366CC>semi-arid climate</color> in the center
• The Himalayas and most of the <color=#3366CC>Hindu Kush</color> have an <color=#3366CC>Alpine climate</color>
Maximum relative humidity of over 80% has been recorded in Khasi and Jaintia Hills and Sri Lanka, while the area
adjustment to Pakistan and western India records lower than 20%–30%. Climate of South Asia is largely characterised
by monsoons. South Asia depends critically on monsoon rainfall. Two monsoon systems exist in the region:
• The summer monsoon: Wind blows from the southwest to most parts of the region. It accounts for 70%–90% of the
annual precipitation.
• The winter monsoon: Wind blows from the northeast. Dominant in Sri Lanka and Maldives.
The warmest period of the year precedes the monsoon season (March to mid June). In the summer the low pressures
are centered over the <color=#3366CC>Indus-Gangetic Plain</color> and high wind from the Indian Ocean blows towards the center. The
monsoons are the second coolest season of the year because of high humidity and cloud covering. But, at the
beginning of June, the jetstreams vanish above the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Plateau</color>, low pressure over the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley</color> deepens and
the <color=#3366CC>Intertropical Convergence Zone</color> (ITCZ) moves in. The change is violent. Moderately vigorous monsoon depressions
form in the Bay of Bengal and make landfall from June to September.
Climate change
South Asian countries are expected to experience more flooding in the future as the monsoon pattern intensifies.
Across Asia as a whole, 100-year extremes in vapour transport (directly related to extreme precipitation) would become
2.6 times more frequent under 1.5 C-change of global warming, yet 3.9 and 7.5 times more frequent under 2 C-change
and 3 C-change. In parts of South Asia, they could become up to 15 times more frequent. At the same time, up to
two-thirds of glacier ice in the Hindu Kush region may melt by 2100 under high warming, and these glaciers feed the
water basin of over 220 million people. As glacier meltwater flow diminishes after 2050, <color=#3366CC>Hydropower</color> generation would
become less predictable and reliable, while agriculture would become more reliant on the intensified monsoon than
ever before. Around 2050, people living in the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and <color=#3366CC>Indus</color> river basins (where up to 60% of non-monsoon
irrigation comes from the glaciers) may be faced with severe water scarcity due to both climate and socioeconomic
reasons.

By 2030, major Indian cities such as <color=#3366CC>Mumbai</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cuttack</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Kochi</color> are expected to end up with much of their
territory below the tide level. In Mumbai alone, failing to adapt to this would result in damages of US$112–162 billion by
2050, which would nearly triple by 2070. <color=#3366CC>Sea level rise</color> in Bangladesh will displace 0.9–2.1 million people by 2050 and
may force the relocation of up to one third of power plants by 2030. <color=#3366CC>Food security</color> will become more uneven, and some
South Asian countries could experience significant social impacts from global food price volatility. <color=#3366CC>Infectious diarrhoea</color>
mortality and <color=#3366CC>dengue fever</color> incidence is also likely to increase across South Asia. Parts of South Asia would also reach
"critical health thresholds" for <color=#3366CC>heat stress</color> under all but the lowest-emission climate change scenarios. Under the
high-emission scenario, 40 million people (nearly 2% of the South Asian population) may be driven to internal migration
by 2050 due to climate change.
India is estimated to have the world's highest social cost of carbon - meaning that it experiences the greatest impact
from <color=#3366CC>greenhouse gas emissions</color>. Other estimates describe Bangladesh as the country most likely to be the
worst-affected. In the 2017 edition of Germanwatch's Climate Risk Index, Bangladesh and Pakistan ranked sixth and
seventh respectively as the countries most affected by climate change in the period from 1996 to 2015, while India
ranked fourth among the list of countries most affected by climate change in 2015. Some research suggests that South
Asia as a whole would lose 2% of its <color=#3366CC>GDP</color> to climate change by 2050, while these losses would approach 9% by the
end of the century under the most intense climate change scenario.
Regions
Northern South Asia
Ethnolinguistically, Northern South Asia is predominantly <color=#3366CC>Indo-Aryan</color>, along with Iranic populations in Afghanistan and
<color=#3366CC>Balochistan</color>, and diverse linguistic communities near the Himalayas. Its borders have been heavily contested (primarily
between India and its neighbours Pakistan and China, as well as separatist movements in Northeast India.) This
tension in the region has contributed to difficulties in sharing river waters among Northern South Asian countries;
climate change is projected to exacerbate the issue. Dominated by the <color=#3366CC>Indo-Gangetic Plain</color>, the region is home to
about half a billion people and is the poorest South Asian subregion.
Northwestern South Asia
Northwestern South Asia is the site of many of the first civilisations of the world, such as the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilisation</color>. It
was historically the most conquered region of South Asia because it is the first region that invading armies coming from
the west had to cross to enter the Indian subcontinent; because of these many invasions, Northwestern South Asia has
significant influences from various sources outside of South Asia, mainly from the <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>.
Eastern South Asia

Eastern South Asia includes <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color>, eastern and <color=#3366CC>northeastern</color> parts of India, and <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>. Major Hindu and
Buddhist kingdoms and empires of the region include Kikata, Videha, Vrji, <color=#3366CC>Magadha</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nanda</color>, Gangaridai, <color=#3366CC>Mauryan</color>,
Anga, Kalinga, Kamarupa, Samatata, Kanva, <color=#3366CC>Gupta</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pala</color>, Gauda, <color=#3366CC>Sena</color>, Khadga, Candra, and Deva. Geographically,
it lies between the Eastern Himalayas and the <color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color>. Two of the world's largest rivers, the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Brahmaputra</color>, flow into the sea through the <color=#3366CC>Bengal region</color>. The region includes the world's largest delta, the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color>

<color=#3366CC>Delta</color>, and has a climate ranging from <color=#3366CC>alpine</color> and <color=#3366CC>subalpine</color> to <color=#3366CC>subtropical</color> and <color=#3366CC>tropical</color>. Since Nepal, Bhutan, Northeast
India and parts of East India are landlocked, the coastlines of Bangladesh and East India (in <color=#3366CC>West Bengal</color> and <color=#3366CC>Odisha</color>)
serve as the principal gateways to the region. With more than 441 million inhabitants, Eastern South Asia is home to
6% of the world's population and 25% of South Asia's population.
Central-West Coastal South Asia
Central South Asia
Southern South Asia

Southern South Asia includes <color=#3366CC>South India</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Maldives</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color>, and is predominantly <color=#3366CC>Dravidian</color>. Southern
South Asia was a hub of global trade in ancient times because of its position in the important Indian Ocean corridor.
Historically, governments throughout Southern South Asia adopted Sanskrit for public political expression beginning
around 300 CE and ending around 1300, resulting in greater integration into the broader <color=#3366CC>Indian cultural sphere</color>. This
significantly influenced the languages of the region, making all of the major Dravidian languages except for Tamil highly
Sanskritised. Tamil influence in the region is quite significant, with prominent empires such as the <color=#3366CC>Chola dynasty</color> taking
Tamil culture to Sri Lanka and beyond South Asia, and Sri Lanka having an ancient Tamil minority and a
Dravidian-influenced majority language of <color=#3366CC>Sinhala</color>.
Land and water area
This list includes <color=#3366CC>dependent territories</color> within their sovereign states (including uninhabited territories), but does not
include claims on <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>. EEZ+TIA is exclusive economic zone (EEZ) plus total internal area (TIA) which includes
land and internal waters.
Society
Population
The population of South Asia is about 1.938 billion which makes it the most populated region in the world. It is socially
very mixed, consisting of many language groups and religions, and social practices in one region that are vastly
different from those in another.
Languages
There are numerous languages in South Asia. The spoken languages of the region are largely based on geography
and shared across religious boundaries, but the written script is sharply divided by religious boundaries. In particular,
Muslims of South Asia such as in Afghanistan and Pakistan use the <color=#3366CC>Arabic alphabet</color> and Persian <color=#3366CC>Nastaliq</color>. Till 1952,
Muslim-majority Bangladesh (then known as East Pakistan) also mandated only the Nastaliq script, but after that
adopted regional scripts and particularly Bengali, after the <color=#3366CC>Language Movement</color> for the adoption of Bengali as the
official language of the then East Pakistan. Non-Muslims of South Asia, and some Muslims in India, on the other hand,
use scripts such as those derived from <color=#3366CC>Brahmi script</color> for Indo-European languages and non-Brahmi scripts for
<color=#3366CC>Dravidian languages</color> and others.
The Nagari script has been the primus inter pares of the traditional South Asian scripts. The <color=#3366CC>Devanagari</color> script is used

for over 120 South Asian languages, including <color=#3366CC>Hindi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Marathi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nepali</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pali</color>, Konkani, Bodo, <color=#3366CC>Sindhi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Maithili</color> among
other languages and dialects, making it one of the most used and adopted writing systems in the world. The
Devanagari script is also used for classical Sanskrit texts.
The largest spoken language in this region is <color=#3366CC>Hindustani language</color>, followed by Bengali, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi,
Gujarati, Kannada, and Punjabi. In the modern era, new syncretic languages developed in the region such as <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color> that
are used by the Muslim community of northern South Asia (particularly Pakistan and northern states of India). The
Punjabi language spans three religions: Islam, Hinduism, and Sikhism. The spoken language is similar, but it is written
in three scripts. The Sikh use Gurmukhi alphabet, Muslim Punjabis in <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> use the <color=#3366CC>Nastaliq script</color>, while Hindu
Punjabis in India use the Gurmukhi or Nāgarī script. The Gurmukhi and Nāgarī scripts are distinct but close in their
structure, but the Persian Nastaliq script is very different.
<color=#3366CC>Sino-Tibetan</color> languages are spoken across northern belts of the region in the <color=#3366CC>Himalayan</color> areas, often using the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan</color>
<color=#3366CC>script</color>. These languages are predominantly spoken in Bhutan and Nepal as well as parts of Burma and northern India in
the state of <color=#3366CC>Sikkim</color> and the Ladakh region. The national language of Bhutan is <color=#3366CC>Dzongkha</color>, while Lepcha, Limbu,
Gurung, Magar, Rai, Newari, Tamang, Tshangla, Thakali, and Sikkimese are also spoken in Bhutan, Nepal and Sikkim,
and Ladakhi is spoken in Ladakh. Both <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bon</color> are often predominant in areas where these languages are
present. Some areas in <color=#3366CC>Gilgit-Baltistan</color> also speak Balti language, however speakers write with the Urdu script. The
Tibetan script fell out of use in Pakistani Baltistan hundreds of years ago upon the region's adoption of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>.
English, with British spelling, is commonly used in urban areas and is a major economic <color=#3366CC>lingua franca</color> of South Asia
(see also South Asian English).
Religions
In 2010, South Asia had the world's largest population of <color=#3366CC>Hindus</color>, about 510 million <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>, over 27 million Sikhs, 35
million <color=#3366CC>Christians</color> and over 25 million Buddhists. Hindus make up about 68% or about 900 million and Muslims at 31%
or 510 million of the overall South Asia population, while Buddhists, Jains, Christians, and Sikhs constitute most of the
rest. The Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, and Christians are concentrated in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Bhutan,
while the Muslims are concentrated in Afghanistan (99%), Bangladesh (90%), Pakistan (96%), and Maldives (100%).
With all major religions practised in the subcontinent, South Asia is known for its religious diversity and one of the most
religiously diverse regions on earth.

<color=#3366CC>Indian religions</color> are the religions that originated in the Indian subcontinent; namely <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>. The Indian religions are distinct yet share terminology, concepts, goals and ideas, and from South Asia spread
into East Asia and Southeast Asia. Early Christianity and Islam were introduced into coastal regions of South Asia by
merchants who settled among the local populations. Later <color=#3366CC>Sindh</color>, <color=#3366CC>Balochistan</color>, and parts of the <color=#3366CC>Punjab region</color> saw
conquest by the <color=#3366CC>Arab caliphates</color> along with an influx of Muslims from Persia and Central Asia, which resulted in spread
of both Shia and Sunni Islam in parts of northwestern region of South Asia. Subsequently, under the influence of
Muslim rulers of the Islamic sultanates and the Mughal Empire, Islam spread in South Asia. About one-third of the
world's Muslims are from South Asia.

Migration
Ancient migrations into South Asia shaped the region's unique demographics, and later migrations often corresponded
with conquest, as with the British diaspora in India.
Contemporary immigration to South Asian countries often takes a uniquely regional form; for example, most migrants in
India are from other South Asian countries, and 97% of Bangladeshi migrants in India live in the Bangladesh-bordering
regions of India (East India and <color=#3366CC>Northeast India</color>).

Economy
India is the largest economy in the region (US$4.18 trillion) and makes up almost 82% of the South Asian economy; it
is the world's 6th largest in nominal terms and the world's 3rd largest by purchasing power adjusted exchange rates
(US$17.64 trillion). India is the member of <color=#3366CC>G-20 major economies</color> and <color=#3366CC>BRICS</color> from the region. It is the fastest-growing
major economy in the world and one of the world's fastest registering a growth of 7.2% in FY 2022–23.
India is followed by Bangladesh, which has a GDP of ($446 billion). It has the fastest GDP growth rate in Asia. It is one
of the emerging and growth-leading economies of the world, and is also listed among the Next Eleven countries. It is
also one of the fastest-growing middle-income countries. It has the world's 33rd largest GDP in nominal terms and is
the 25th largest by purchasing power adjusted exchange rates ($1.476 trillion). Bangladesh's economic growth was
6.4% in 2022. The next one is Pakistan, which has an economy of ($340 billion). Next is <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color>, which has the 2nd
highest GDP per capita and the 4th largest economy in the region. According to a <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> report in 2015, driven by
a strong expansion in India, coupled with favourable oil prices, from the last quarter of 2014 South Asia became the
fastest-growing region in the world.
While in East Asia, regional trade accounts for 50% of total trade, it accounts for only a little more than 5% in South
Asia. Certain parts of South Asia are significantly wealthier than others; the four Indian states of <color=#3366CC>Maharashtra</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tamil</color>

<color=#3366CC>Nadu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gujarat</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Karnataka</color> are projected to account for almost 50% of India's GDP by 2030, while the five <color=#3366CC>South</color>
<color=#3366CC>Indian states</color> comprising 20% of India's population are expected to contribute 35% of India's GDP by 2030.
Poverty
According to the World Bank's 2011 report, based on 2005 ICP PPP, about 24.6% of the South Asian population was
below the international poverty line of $1.25/day. Bhutan, Maldives and Sri Lanka had the lowest number of people
below the poverty line, with 2.4%, 1.5% and 4.1% respectively.
According to the 2023 MPI (multidimensional poverty index) report by the UN, around 20% of South Asians are poor.
51.7% of Afghanistan's population was under the MPI poverty threshold in 2019, while 24.1% of Bangladesh's
population was under the threshold in 2021. India lifted 415 million people from MPI-poverty from 2005/06 to 2019/21;
16.4% of India's population was MPI-poor in 2019/2021, compared to 55.1% in 2005/2006. 10% of India's population
was under the international poverty line of $2.15/day in 2021.
